domain: Health Systems / Labor Economics / Organizational Behavior
topic_summary: Analysis of Chen et al. 2026 AMA study documenting early clinical departure among U.S. physicians. Survey of 971 clinically inactive physicians (residency completion 2000-2022) reveals mean departure age dropped from 57.1 (2008) to 48.1 (2024), with 11% never entering practice post-residency. Primary drivers shifted from malpractice/health concerns to burnout, administrative burden, and unrealistic patient expectations. Gender disparity: women exit after median 9 years vs 12 for men, 43% higher departure rate across all ages.

key_entities: Concierge/direct primary care models (market alternative, 80% growth 2018-2023)
Association of American Medical Colleges (workforce projection authority)
Female physicians (2/3 of departures, 43% higher exit rate)
key_claims: Mean departure age fell 9 years (57.1→48.1) between 2008-2024
Top departure reasons: hassle factor 44.7%, stress 44.5%, unrealistic patient demands 41.1%
11% of residency-trained physicians never entered clinical practice
Women exit 3 years earlier (median 9 vs 12 years) with 43% higher departure rate
Projected physician shortage of 40,000 by 2036 despite pipeline expansion
Concierge medicine growth (80% 2018-2023) as market signal of system failure
33% of medical groups lost a physician to burnout in past year (MGMA 2026)
key_tensions: Pipeline expansion (new medical schools, residency slots) vs accelerating mid-career attrition
Patient demand for comprehensive care vs time-constrained visit structure
Physician autonomy/professional satisfaction vs administrative burden/EHR requirements
Gender-neutral training pipeline vs gendered caregiving burden driving differential exit
key_mechanisms: Burnout cascade: administrative burden → chronic stress → early departure (feedback loop)
Market bypass: physicians exit traditional employment → concierge/DPC models (80% growth)
Training investment loss: 11% residency completion → immediate non-entry (sunk cost)
key_absences: No analysis of specialty-specific departure rates (data collected but not reported)
No financial modeling of training investment loss (11% non-entry + early departure)
No comparison to other high-skill professions with similar training investment (law, engineering)

axes.human_readable: Administrative Extraction Ratchet (EHR/Documentation Burden as Structural Tax)
axes.structural_delta: Increasing non-clinical documentation requirements that extract time from patient care without corresponding reduction in clinical workload
axes.primary_observable: Hours per week on EHR/administrative tasks; ratio of documentation time to patient contact time; inbox message volume
axes.selection_reason: Highest-epsilon snare with 2 outbound edges; 'hassle factor' (44.7%) operationalizes as measurable administrative burden

axes.human_readable: Patient Expectation Inflation (Demand Expansion Without Resource Expansion)
axes.structural_delta: Patient expectations for comprehensive, immediate, always-available care exceed structural capacity of visit-based care model
axes.primary_observable: Patient portal message volume; after-hours contact attempts; multi-problem visit frequency; patient satisfaction scores vs physician burnout scores
axes.selection_reason: Independent observable from axis 1 (patient-side demand vs system-side documentation); 41.1% cite unrealistic demands; tangled_rope captures coordination failure

axes.human_readable: Gendered Caregiving Penalty (Differential Exit via Unpaid Labor Collision)
axes.structural_delta: Women physicians face structural collision between clinical workload and disproportionate unpaid caregiving responsibilities, producing 43% higher exit rate
axes.primary_observable: Gender-stratified departure rates; median career length by gender; cited reasons (caregiving responsibilities); hours spent on household/childcare labor
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (gender-stratified exit rates) with independent ε; 43% higher departure rate is structural, not preference-based

axes.human_readable: Burnout as Structural Outcome (Chronic Stress as Downstream Synthesis)
axes.structural_delta: Burnout is not a psychological failure but the predictable outcome of sustained extraction via administrative burden, patient demand inflation, and caregiving collision
axes.primary_observable: Burnout prevalence rates; correlation between administrative burden/patient demands and burnout scores; departure timing relative to burnout onset
axes.selection_reason: Highest centrality (3 inbound, 2 outbound); downstream synthesis node; 44.5% cite 'too stressful' as direct manifestation

axes.human_readable: Early Departure Age Collapse (9-Year Forward Shift in Exit Timing)
axes.structural_delta: Mean departure age fell from 57.1 (2008) to 48.1 (2024), representing structural acceleration of career truncation
axes.primary_observable: Mean/median departure age over time; years of clinical practice before exit; age distribution of departing physicians
axes.selection_reason: Mountain capturing observable outcome; distinct from mechanism (burnout) and distinct from non-entry; feeds workforce crisis

axes.structural_delta: 11% of residency-trained physicians never enter clinical practice, representing complete training investment loss before career start
axes.primary_observable: Percentage of residency graduates not entering practice; timing of exit decision relative to residency completion; specialty distribution of non-entrants
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable from early departure (exit before vs during career); piton captures atrophied function (training pipeline that doesn't produce clinicians)

axes.human_readable: Workforce Pipeline Paradox (Expansion at Intake, Hemorrhage at Output)
axes.structural_delta: System expands medical school/residency capacity while losing physicians at both ends (11% non-entry + accelerating mid-career exit), producing net workforce contraction despite input growth
axes.primary_observable: Medical school enrollment trends; residency slot expansion; net physician workforce change; projected shortage (40,000 by 2036) despite pipeline growth
axes.selection_reason: Downstream synthesis of workforce crisis; captures policy failure (expanding intake while ignoring retention); 2 inbound edges

axes.human_readable: Market Bypass Mechanism (Concierge/DPC as Extraction Escape)
axes.structural_delta: Physicians exit traditional employment for concierge/direct primary care models (80% growth 2018-2023) to escape administrative burden and restore clinical autonomy
axes.primary_observable: Concierge/DPC practice growth rates; physician migration from traditional to alternative models; patient panel size reduction; administrative burden comparison
axes.selection_reason: Distinct observable (practice model migration) with independent ε; rope captures coordination mechanism (physicians + patients jointly exit); market signal of system failure

omegas.description: Study collected specialty-specific departure data but did not report it. Primary care vs procedural specialties may have structurally different ε values for administrative burden and patient expectation axes. Absence of stratification may mask specialty-specific snares.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + extraction_summary absence 1

omegas.description: No financial modeling of sunk cost: 11% non-entry + early departure (9 years earlier) represents massive training investment loss. Is this a Piton (atrophied medical education ROI) or a Mountain (unavoidable given labor market structure)? Quantification would clarify.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + extraction_summary absence 2

omegas.description: No comparison to law, engineering, or other high-skill professions with similar training investment. Is physician departure rate structurally higher, or is this a general high-skill labor market phenomenon? Absence of comparison limits causal attribution.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (Absence Inventory) + extraction_summary absence 3

omegas.description: Is market_bypass_mechanism a stable Rope (sustainable alternative model) or a Scaffold (temporary arbitrage that collapses when concierge market saturates)? 80% growth may be early-phase bubble. Longitudinal data needed.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 3 (Beneficiary Scan) + axis classification uncertainty

omegas.description: Patient expectation inflation axis does not identify upstream driver. Is it a Rope (coordination failure) or downstream of a Snare (insurance/regulatory structure that incentivizes patient maximalism)? Causal direction unclear from study data.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Eight axes survived independence testing with distinct observables and ε values. Specialty stratification absence noted in omega but does not constitute F15 (study collected data; reporting choice, not analytical closure). Gender axis passes independence test (distinct observable: gender-stratified exit rates; distinct ε: caregiving collision vs administrative burden).
